differences.title: 1. ARCHITECTURE
differences.leftDesc: Valkey runs an in-memory data engine with optional persistence. Typical Redis-style workloads hit a single leader process per node, scaling primarily via client sharding or clustering layers.
differences.rightDesc: Aerospike is designed around a distributed, partitioned architecture where data is sharded by digest across nodes. Each node manages its own partitions, enabling horizontal scaling with predictable access patterns.

differences.title: 2. DATA MODEL & OPERATIONS
differences.leftDesc: Valkey supports Redis-style structures (strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, streams) plus rich command semantics. Many operations are implemented as single-threaded command handlers per node.
differences.rightDesc: Aerospike is centered on a fast key-value store with bins (fields) per record. It supports server-side UDFs and atomic bin updates, prioritizing low-latency reads/writes over deep secondary structures.

differences.title: 3. STORAGE LAYOUT
differences.leftDesc: Valkey keeps hot keys in RAM and optionally uses RDB snapshots and/or AOF-style append logging for durability. Restart recovery reconstructs the keyspace from persisted artifacts.
differences.rightDesc: Aerospike uses a memory-first design with configurable storage engine behavior, keeping primary working sets in RAM and using SSD for elastic capacity. Record metadata and caching policies reduce disk reads.

differences.title: 4. REPLICATION & CONSISTENCY
differences.leftDesc: Valkey typically uses replication for high availability (one primary with replicas). Consistency depends on write acknowledgment behavior and client routing to primaries, with eventual propagation to replicas.
differences.rightDesc: Aerospike supports configurable replication factor and consistency levels using quorum-like semantics. Reads/writes can be acknowledged from specific nodes/sets, balancing latency against durability requirements.

differences.title: 5. DISTRIBUTED SCALING MECHANISM
differences.leftDesc: Valkey scaling often relies on Redis Cluster-style sharding where keys map to hash slots across nodes. Rebalancing moves slots, and client libraries must route based on slot map.
differences.rightDesc: Aerospike automatically determines partition ownership via cluster metadata and consistent hashing of digests. Rebalancing reassigns partitions and streams data, while clients can use policies to stay fast through topology changes.

differences.title: 6. EXPIRATION & EVICTION
differences.rightDesc: Aerospike uses per-record TTLs plus storage-engine aware eviction and background management. Its policy engine considers namespaces, sets, and memory/disk tiers to limit impact on read latency.
differences.leftDesc: Valkey implements TTLs per key and supports eviction strategies (e.g., allkeys-lru, volatile-lru) when memory limits are hit. Expired keys are removed via active and lazy mechanisms.

differences.title: 7. LATENCY TARGETS & ATOMICITY
differences.leftDesc: Valkey guarantees atomic execution of each command within the server process. Multi-key operations require Lua scripting, transactions, or careful client-side orchestration to maintain atomic semantics across keys.
differences.rightDesc: Aerospike provides strong atomicity at the record/bin level: updates to a record can be applied atomically even under concurrency. UDFs and atomic operations reduce race windows for hot keys.
